new_statements.quote: Note.—Mention may be conveniently made here of certain words which although they appear to be identical with Kiswahili or other languages differ as regards stress :— Dog is mbúa, not mbwa. Mosquito is mbúu, not mbu. Face is usíu, not uso. Head is mtúe, not mtwe. New (adjective) is -pía (as in the northern dialects of Swahili), not -pya, etc.
new_statements.citation: Johnson, Frederick. 1923-1926. Notes on Kiniramba. Bantu Studies 2: 167-192, 233-268.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote: opened, PDF page 6 = printed p. 172 (running head 'FREDERICK JOHNSON—'); rendered the page image at 150 dpi and read it: the Note under 'Class 14 (originally identical with 11)' reads exactly as quoted, and the acute accents on mbúa, mbúu, usíu, mtúe, -pía are present in print (the extracted text layer garbles them, so the image is the check). Surrounding section: the 'Alphabet' section (pp. 168-169, PDF pp. 2-3) lists five vowels and the consonants, notes on r/l, g/k, s/sh, aspiration per Ittameier, and says nothing about stress, tone or length. A grep of the whole 62-page extract finds 'stress' only in this Note; the only other prosodic remarks are A. Werner's editorial footnotes '…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened states a stress-placement rule. Johnson's only remark on stress is incidental: in five words whose Swahili cognates have a glide (mbwa, mbu, uso, mtwe, -pya), Kiniramba has a vowel sequence with the stress (acute) on the first vowel of the sequence, i.e. on the penult (mbú-a, mbú-u, u-sí-u, mtú-e, -pí-a). That is consistent with penultimate prominence but is not stated as a rule and no other word in the article or vocabulary carries a stress mark. The modern first-hand description, Yukawa 1989 (p. 406, saved), treats Nilamba purely as an H/L tone language ('we shall put ´ on a vowel or homorganic nasal pronounced high and nothing on a low one') with sentence-final falling/rising-tone realisations on the final and penultimate syllables, and never mentions stress; Ngwasi 2021 (§4.2.4) likewise reports lexical tone (nzala 'hunger' vs nzála 'fingers') and a vowel-length contrast, no stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Johnson's forms are citation forms of isolated words; Yukawa's tone description covers verb forms in isolation and at sentence end (phrase-final penultimate rising tone is a phrasal phenomenon, not word stress).
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the same language: Johnson's 'Kiniramba' of the Iramba plateau (Tanganyika), Yukawa's 'Nilamba (kinilamba)' from a Singida-born speaker, Ngwasi's Nilamba (F31) = Glottolog nila1242 / ISO nim. Masele 2001 distinguishes a 'Kinilamba central' dialect but none of the stress/tone remarks are dialect-specific.

sources.quote: Note.—Mention may be conveniently made here of certain words which although they appear to be identical with Kiswahili or other languages differ as regards stress :— Dog is mbúa, not mbwa. Mosquito is mbúu, not mbu. Face is usíu, not uso. Head is mtúe, not mtwe. New (adjective) is -pía (as in the northern dialects of Swahili), not -pya, etc.
sources.note: 'Alphabet' section (pp. 168-169) gives only segments; no stress or tone rule. Sole stress remark is an incidental Note on p. 172 listing words that 'differ as regards stress' from Swahili, with acute accents on the penultimate vowel of final vowel sequences (mbúa, mbúu, usíu, mtúe, -pía). Editorial footnotes (A. Werner) ask whether homophones are 'distinguished by tone'; vocabulary marks no stress or tone.

sources.citation: Ngwasi, Lengson. 2021. The multiple functions of the reflexive prefix in Hehe, Sukuma, Nilamba, and Nyaturu. PhD thesis, University of Gothenburg. https://gupea.ub.gu.se/handle/2077/69663
sources.note: §4.2.2 vowel length contrast in all four languages; §4.2.4 Tone: Nilamba has lexical H/L tone (nzala 'hunger' vs nzála 'fingers', citing Nicodemus 2013: 7) and tone deletion in verbs (citing Yukawa 1989b). No stress statement. Its literature review (pp. 12-13) lists all known Nilamba descriptions: Johnson 1923a/b, Ittameier 1922, Yukawa 1989a/b, Nicodemus 2013 (MA UDSM), Mdima 2000 (BA UDSM), Masele 2001, Nurse 1979.

sources.citation: Yukawa, Yasutoshi. 1989. A tonological study of Nilamba verbs. In R. Kagaya, R. M. Besha & Y. Yukawa (eds.), Studies in Tanzanian languages, 405-449. Tokyo: ILCAA (TUFS). hdl:10108/93051.
sources.note: Treats Nilamba as an H/L tone language: acute on high vowels/nasals, nothing on low (p. 406); describes sentence-final falling/rising-tone realisations on the final and penultimate syllables (p. 406 and notes 19-23, pp. 448-449). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the 45 pages (full-text grep of scanned).
